# Stacks & Queues in Lua

Two of the simplest data structures, and two of the most used:

- A **stack** is last in, first out, like a pile of plates. Undo, the browser's back button and every function call your program makes run on stacks.
- A **queue** is first in, first out, like a line at a till. Print jobs, network packets and tasks waiting for a processor run in queues.

Lua has exactly one data structure, the **table**, and it is enough for both. The questions: **how does a stack know brackets are balanced, and how does a queue run for ever in a fixed amount of memory?**

How the cells run:

- **Lua runs in your browser** (Wasmoon, Lua 5.4), and shares what it did by printing `__NB_SET__` lines.
- **Two HTML cells** play each run back step by step; **JavaScript** compares two ways to share a printer.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 1. A stack that checks brackets

> In Lua, write a stack as a table with push and pop, and use it to check whether the brackets in a text are balanced: push each opener, and on each closer pop and check it is the matching opener. Record every push and pop with the stack after it, plus a last step saying done, leftover or mismatch. Check (a[b]{c}), ([)], function f() return {1, 2} end, if (x[1] > 0 then and {{[[(())]]}}, print the verdicts, and publish nb.brackets = [{text, ok, steps: [{i, action, stack}]}] with a `__NB_SET__` line.

- **`Stack`** is a table and a `top` counter. `push` adds at `top + 1`; `pop` takes from `top`. Both take one step however big the stack is.
- **Why a stack?** The most recent unclosed opener is the one the next closer must match: last in, first out.
- **Two ways to fail**: a closer meets the wrong opener (`mismatch`), or the text ends with openers still waiting (`leftover`).

-- A stack is just a table used from one end.
local Stack = {}
Stack.__index = Stack

function Stack.new()
  return setmetatable({ items = {}, top = 0 }, Stack)
end

function Stack:push(v)
  self.top = self.top + 1
  self.items[self.top] = v
end

function Stack:pop()
  if self.top == 0 then return nil end
  local v = self.items[self.top]
  self.items[self.top] = nil
  self.top = self.top - 1
  return v
end

local function json(s)          -- a Lua string as a JSON string
  return '"' .. s:gsub('\\', '\\\\'):gsub('"', '\\"') .. '"'
end

-- Classic stack job: are the brackets balanced? Records every push and pop.
local openers = { ["("] = true, ["["] = true, ["{"] = true }
local match = { [")"] = "(", ["]"] = "[", ["}"] = "{" }

local function balanced(s, steps)
  local st = Stack.new()
  local function record(i, action)
    local copy = {}
    for k = 1, st.top do copy[k] = json(st.items[k]) end
    steps[#steps + 1] = string.format('{"i":%d,"action":"%s","stack":[%s]}', i, action, table.concat(copy, ","))
  end
  for i = 1, #s do
    local ch = s:sub(i, i)
    if openers[ch] then
      st:push(ch)
      record(i, "push")
    elseif match[ch] then
      local top = st:pop()
      if top ~= match[ch] then
        record(i, "mismatch")
        return false
      end
      record(i, "pop")
    end
  end
  record(#s, st.top == 0 and "done" or "leftover")
  return st.top == 0
end

local tests = {
  "(a[b]{c})",
  "([)]",
  "function f() return {1, 2} end",
  "if (x[1] > 0 then",
  "{{[[(())]]}}",
}

local results = {}
for _, s in ipairs(tests) do
  local steps = {}
  local ok = balanced(s, steps)
  results[#results + 1] = string.format('{"text":%s,"ok":%s,"steps":[%s]}', json(s), tostring(ok), table.concat(steps, ","))
  print(string.format("%-34s %-13s %d stack steps", s, ok and "balanced" or "NOT balanced", #steps))
end

print('__NB_SET__ {"key":"brackets","value":[' .. table.concat(results, ",") .. ']}')

## 3. A queue that goes round

> In Lua, write a ring buffer: a fixed number of slots, a read position and a count, where the write position is read + count and both wrap round with %. Use one with 4 slots as a print spooler for thesis.pdf (12 pages), photo.png (2), report.docx (7) and ticket.pdf (1), printing 5 pages a tick and putting unfinished jobs back at the end (round-robin). Snapshot the slots, read position and count after every tick with a sentence, print each tick, and publish nb.spool = {capacity, pagesPerTick, jobs, frames, finished: [{name, tick}]} with a `__NB_SET__` line.

- **A plain table queue** that removes from the front with `table.remove(t, 1)` shifts every item along, every time.
- **A ring buffer** never moves anything: it moves the read position instead, and when a position runs off the end, `% capacity` brings it back to slot 0. Four slots serve the spooler for as long as it runs.
- **Round-robin**: each job gets at most 5 pages, then goes to the back, so a short job never waits for a long one to finish.

-- A ring buffer: a fixed number of slots, a read position and a count.
-- Positions wrap round with %, so nothing ever shuffles along.
local Ring = {}
Ring.__index = Ring

function Ring.new(capacity)
  return setmetatable({ slots = {}, capacity = capacity, first = 0, count = 0 }, Ring)
end

function Ring:enqueue(v)
  if self.count == self.capacity then return false end   -- full
  local at = (self.first + self.count) % self.capacity
  self.slots[at + 1] = v
  self.count = self.count + 1
  return true
end

function Ring:dequeue()
  if self.count == 0 then return nil end
  local v = self.slots[self.first + 1]
  self.slots[self.first + 1] = nil
  self.first = (self.first + 1) % self.capacity
  self.count = self.count - 1
  return v
end

-- A print spooler: 5 pages per tick, unfinished jobs go to the back (round-robin).
local PAGES_PER_TICK = 5
local jobs = {
  { name = "thesis.pdf",  pages = 12 },
  { name = "photo.png",   pages = 2 },
  { name = "report.docx", pages = 7 },
  { name = "ticket.pdf",  pages = 1 },
}
local q = Ring.new(4)
for _, j in ipairs(jobs) do q:enqueue({ name = j.name, pages = j.pages }) end

local frames = {}
local function snapshot(tick, say)
  local slots = {}
  for k = 1, q.capacity do
    local job = q.slots[k]
    slots[k] = job and string.format('{"name":"%s","pages":%d}', job.name, job.pages) or "null"
  end
  frames[#frames + 1] = string.format('{"tick":%d,"first":%d,"count":%d,"slots":[%s],"say":"%s"}',
    tick, q.first, q.count, table.concat(slots, ","), say)
end
snapshot(0, "4 jobs waiting in a ring of 4 slots")

local tick, finished = 0, {}
while q.count > 0 do
  tick = tick + 1
  local job = q:dequeue()
  local printed = math.min(PAGES_PER_TICK, job.pages)
  job.pages = job.pages - printed
  local say
  if job.pages > 0 then
    q:enqueue(job)
    say = string.format("%s: printed %d, %d left, back of the queue", job.name, printed, job.pages)
  else
    finished[#finished + 1] = string.format('{"name":"%s","tick":%d}', job.name, tick)
    say = string.format("%s: printed %d, done", job.name, printed)
  end
  print(string.format("tick %d: %s", tick, say))
  snapshot(tick, say)
end

local jobJson = {}
for k, j in ipairs(jobs) do jobJson[k] = string.format('{"name":"%s","pages":%d}', j.name, j.pages) end
print('__NB_SET__ {"key":"spool","value":{"capacity":4,"pagesPerTick":' .. PAGES_PER_TICK ..
  ',"jobs":[' .. table.concat(jobJson, ",") .. '],"frames":[' .. table.concat(frames, ",") ..
  '],"finished":[' .. table.concat(finished, ",") .. ']}}')

## 5. Is round-robin fair?

> In JavaScript, check the spooler and compare policies: simulate nb.spool.jobs yourself with round-robin (an unfinished job goes to the back) and first-come-first-served (it keeps the printer until done), check the round-robin matches the Lua run, and print a table of each job's finish tick under both and the average. Then return a Vega-Lite line chart of the average finish tick against pages per tick, 1 to 12, for both policies.

Round-robin feels fair, but is it faster? This cell runs the same four jobs both ways, at every printer speed from 1 to 12 pages a tick, and checks its own round-robin against the Lua run.

## What the run shows

- **The stack catches what counting can't.** `([)]` has one of each bracket, but the `)` pops `[`: a mismatch at step 3. `if (x[1] > 0 then` fails the other way, ending with `(` still on the stack. `{{[[(())]]}}` is balanced, with the stack 6 deep at its peak.
- **Four slots run the whole spooler.** The read position goes round the ring 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, …; unfinished jobs go back in at the write position. Nothing in the ring is ever moved.
- **Round-robin lets short jobs out early.** At 5 pages a tick, photo.png (2 pages) finishes at tick 2 and ticket.pdf (1 page) at tick 4; served first-come, first-served they would wait until ticks 4 and 7 behind the 12-page thesis. The thesis pays: tick 7 instead of 3.
- **On average it's a little faster, and much faster on a slow printer.** The average finish tick is 4.75 against 5.00 at 5 pages a tick; at 1 page a tick it is 12.25 against 17.25. Once a tick prints 7 pages or more, nearly every job fits in one turn and the two policies are the same. At 6 pages a tick round-robin is slightly worse, 4.25 against 4.00: the thesis and the report each need just one more turn, and sending them to the back for it costs them more than it saves the short jobs.
- **JavaScript agrees with Lua.** Its own round-robin gives exactly the Lua run's finish ticks.
